title: Serve where you can
hook: if public life is closed, serve privately, as Athenodorus advised (On Tranquility 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fleeing yourself, the sleepless turning over and over. Your line was stay put.

Maybe you once wanted to change the world. Run for office, lead the charity, fix the system. Then life happened: the job, the kids, the illness, the door that closed. Now the big stage feels shut. So is there any point? Seneca's next chapter takes up exactly this. After stay put, the obvious worry is: stay put and do what? His answer starts with a philosopher named Athenodorus, who had thought hard about what to do when public life becomes impossible, and whose advice Seneca passes on, and then argues with.
screen: `THE BIG STAGE FEELS SHUT.` → `STAY PUT AND DO WHAT?` → `ATHENODORUS HAS AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, Athenodorus' advice. The best cure for restlessness, he says, is useful work: public duties, the life of a citizen. But the forum is full of ambition and slander, and an honest person can be shut out. Then don't sulk. Serve privately, with your advice, your voice, your example. Someone who steadies a friend or teaches a young person is still serving the city. Second, Seneca pushes back a little. He thinks Athenodorus gives up the public stage too fast. Don't run, Seneca says. Retreat slowly, like a soldier giving ground with the flag still up. If you can't fight in the front line, hold your place in the ranks. If you can't hold a place, shout encouragement. There's always some post. Third, his example. Seneca brings back Socrates, from day four hundred eighty-two: when Athens was ruled by the Thirty Tyrants, Socrates still walked the city, encouraging the frightened and calming the despairing. No office. Just presence. Fourth, the week. Mind the gap. Hard compromises. Flawed and wise. Write back. Neither sick nor well. Stay put. A whole week about a life that didn't go to plan, Seneca's own included. And the answer here isn't grand. When the big stage is closed, a small one is always open: one conversation, one errand, one person on the other end of a phone.
screen: `ATHENODORUS: SERVE PRIVATELY.` · `SENECA: RETREAT SLOWLY, FLAG UP.` · `SOCRATES UNDER THE THIRTY.` · `A SMALL STAGE IS ALWAYS OPEN.` · then, large: `SERVE WHERE I CAN.`

segments.voice: Think of the big thing you once hoped to do, and let yourself feel whatever's left of it. Now shrink it: if you wanted to fix education, one young person you could encourage; if you wanted to heal people, one person who'd be glad of a call; if you wanted justice, one small fair thing within reach. Pick one, and picture doing it quietly, with nobody watching.
Officium. Latin for duty, service: Athenodorus' advice, sharpened by Seneca, for when the public stage closes, serve in private, and never desert your post entirely. Today's word.
Your line: serve where i can. There's always some post, even when the big stage is shut. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: People drawing on Seneca often look for a small, private way to be useful when larger public roles are closed to them, such as mentoring, advising or helping one person.

chat.meaning: Athenodorus says serve privately when public life shuts. Seneca adds: retreat slowly, flag up; if you can't fight, shout encouragement. There's always some post.

Athenodorus.meaning: a philosopher whose advice on serving privately Seneca passes on

forum.meaning: the public square at the center of Roman public life

Thirty Tyrants.meaning: the harsh rulers Athens fell under in Socrates' time

Socrates.meaning: the Athenian philosopher who kept encouraging people under the Thirty
